newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE - Foreign banks build up Tokyo finance houses.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Foreign banks build up Tokyo finance houses.

text.p: Foreign bankers, particularly Europeans, are beefing up their Tokyo operations to meet demand for sophisticated financial instruments after cutting back on expensive Japanese offices a few years ago.

But while the brain-drain from Tokyo financial markets known as "hollowing" appears to have abated or even reversed, some U.S. institutions are going the other way -- a vacuum European competitors are only too happy to fill.

"Other banks are rationalising or moving away...This gives us a chance to go in the front door of a lot of companies where we weren't able to go before," said Chris Pavlou, treasurer at HSBC Midland Bank Plc's Tokyo branch.

Britain-based HSBC Midland is planning substantial personnel increases over the next 18 months, while fellow HSBC Group member HSBC Securities Ltd plans to double its staff in Tokyo over a similar period, Pavlou told Reuters.

Most of the effort is going into sophisticated instruments for which bankers detect an increasing appetite among Japanese investors. Costs are also playing a role as the weaker yen is making Tokyo a less prohibitive base for Asian operations.
NO ONE CAN IGNORE TOKYO
Tokyo may now be little more expensive than rival Asian financial capitals like Singapore or Hong Kong.
And no one can ignore the size of its capital markets.

"We tend to forget in the U.S. that two-thirds of the Asian GDP is here in Japan...This is still the second major player in financial markets. The sun is not setting here," said Robert D. Hormats, Vice Chairman, Goldman Sachs (International).

HSBC Securities plans to double to 50 people from 25. Currency options personnel at Midland will double to 10, while the bank's foreign exchange staff will increase to roughly 30 from 22, said HSBC Midland's Pavlou.

France's Societe Generale has increased its Tokyo staff to 15 from 9 and extended foreign exchange trading time to 24 hours in September, while BNP Securities Japan, securities arm of French-based Banque Nationale de Paris, said that it plans to nearly double its Tokyo staff by the year 2000.
Other major European banks are also known to be strongly beefing up their personnel, particularly in such areas as options and capital markets.
The Japanese Ministry of Finance which had been nervous and the exodus of talent from the Tokyo banking sector, welcomes the return of the Europeans to reinforce Tokyo's status.

"I feel this is something that should be very highly welcomed," said a senior ministry official. "We at the Ministry were concerned about this issue (of hollowing), and made efforts, and now we're seeing a bit of the results."
The finance ministry has played its part by promoting deregulation of the foreign exchange trade.
CUSTOMERS SEEK NEW FINANCIAL INSTRUMENTS

Various reasons are cited for the expansion, but key among them appears to be the increasing appetite for new financial products from Japanese corporate clients, many of whom now have a greater need to hedge risks as offshore business increases.
"Our customers are getting more sophisticated, and they need more tools to hedge their risks," said Midland's Pavlou.

"Japanese investors are looking for more "high-tech' products, and there is an increasing demand for these," said Mariko Terazaki, public affairs manager for the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corp, flagship of the HSBC group.
An economist at a European bank, who declined to be named, agreed that options interest is definitely on the rise, and not just in "plain vanilla" products such as dollar spot options.

"Because most of our counterparts in this activity are Japanese corporations who want to do their trade in yen, and prefer to do it face-to-face as well as by phone, it is good to have a strong presence in Tokyo," he added.

Other incentives are the yen's depreciation against the dollar and rising office costs in other Asian centres, said Ryosuke Tsuji, senior vice president and manager of the Spot Foreign Exchange department at Societe Generale.
"Some foreign banks have been shifting operations overseas because of lower costs, but the major currency in Asia is still the yen and the most liquidity is here in Tokyo," he said.
POLITICAL STABILITY A FACTOR
Until recently a strong yen, combined with high building rents and personnel costs, caused many operators to move all or part of their operations to less expensive centres overseas.

Tsuji noted that the yen's fall, which has seen it at 112 yen to the dollar recently compared to a record high of 79.75 yen in April 1995, along with rises in asset prices and office costs in rivals like Hong Kong and Singapore, made them almost as high as Tokyo, suggesting Japan is no longer so expensive.
Some dealers hinted at other reasons for the Tokyo buildup. Said one: "There is a bit of a feeling that Tokyo may be a more politically stable market (than others) in the future."
But some U.S. institutions are cutting back due mainly to low profit outlook for the Japanese stock market.
Citicorp International Securities Ltd, a subsidiary of Citicorp, said in August that it will end trade in Japanese shares and exchange-traded equities futures and options.
Said Kenro Arimoto, director and Tokyo manager: "Equities business could not be our core business in the past and we think it will not be core business in the future, either."

Dealers in Singapore took a mixed view of any shift to Tokyo. A dealer with a Japanese bank there said banks were shifting some operations to Tokyo, such as proprietary trading for yen products, as the market is more liquid for yen there.
"To run Japanese yen products out of Singapore doesn't really pay off," he said.
HSBC BUILDS FOR FUTURE
Meanwhile Hongkong Bank plans to build a new 10-storey building in Tokyo's business district, believing that the largest market in Asia has to be the place to be.

"Yes, Hong Kong and Singapore are very good markets, they are very exciting and they are more open, but we find that the Tokyo market is the largest in Asia. The economy will probably pick up, and we want to be ready to take part when it happens," said Hongkong and Shanghai's Terazaki.
